newsitem.title: HAITI: Haitians protest against United Nations peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: Haitians protest against United Nations peacekeepers.

text.p: Demonstrators burned tires and threw rocks at United Nations peacekeepers and many Haitians stayed home on Monday in response to a call for a general strike to protest the presence of foreign troops.
"Hit the road! Go home!" onlookers yelled at passing Canadian U.N. peacekeepers.

The call by grassroots political organisations for a national strike was respected to varying degrees throughout Haiti, with reports of tires burning in the northern city of Cap-Haitien and deserted streets in some smaller cities.
Some businesses in the capital were closed but as the day wore on, activity in the streets picked up. There were no reports of serious violence or injuries.
"Everything is basically peaceful," U.N. spokeswoman Patricia Tome said.

The U.N. Security Council was expected to vote this week on whether the troops will stay in Haiti four months past the current July 31 deadline. An extension would be the latest in a series that has maintained a U.N. presence since March 1995.

The U.N. troops took over the work of securing Haiti from 20,000 U.S. troops who restored then-president Jean-Bertrand Aristide to power in the fall of 1994, three years after he had been ousted in a bloody military coup.
A growing number of Haitians have referred to the foreign presence as an occupation and are frustrated the peacekeepers have been ordered not to intervene in Haitian disputes or violence.

"Those guys are on vacation," a 28-year-old Haitian watching troops pass on a main street of the capital said. "They don't do anything to provide security, except to guard the Palace and Aristide's house."
President Rene Preval and many Haitians support the extension, saying the Haitian National Police force is not yet ready to maintain security.
Bill Richardson, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations, said this month that Aristide, who still wields considerable popular power, supported Preval's request for an extension.

But a political source who was at a recent meeting between Aristide and Richardson said the support was conditional. "Aristide said he would support Preval's decision but that the relationship of the U.N. troops to the population needs to be discussed," the source said.

That relationship came under scrutiny two weeks ago when U.N. Civilian Police trainer Ian Belley arrested a local official in the northern city of Port-de-Paix in front of a crowd of witnesses. The official had asked Belley move his car out of the road, according to witnesses.
Belley had to be removed by helicopter when an angry crowd gathered. The U.N. mission issued an official apology.
While Aristide has remained quiet on the mandate issue, a Senate candidate from Aristide's Fanmi Lavalas party has come out against the foreign presence.
"It's clear they ought to leave the country," Yvon Feuille told Radio Metropole.
Some observers said the grassroots groups that called the strike were Aristide supporters, noting anti-U.N. graffiti was recently scrawled throughout the capital along with pro-Fanmi Lavalas slogans.
Lower House President Kely Bastien wrote a letter to Preval questioning his request for an extended U.N. mission.
"In only four months, will the U.N. be able to resolve all that it could not accomplish in two years?" he asked. "If so, what is the strategy they propose?"
